explanations.explanation: Yes, friend, he says he's reciting his verses to the king. His heart is stirred by a noble theme, and he calls his tongue "the pen of a skillful writer." (Psalm 45:1) Imagine having that much confidence in your own handwriting. I can't even stamp straight on a Monday.

Nope, no priests in this verse. The writer says, "I recite my verses to the king…" (Psalm 45:1) The song is written for the choirmaster, but the poem itself is aimed at the king. Priests aren't on the guest list in this one.

Close, but the elders don't show up in this verse. The writer says he recites his verses "to the king…" (Psalm 45:1) He's got one audience in mind, and it wears a crown. So when you hear this psalm, think king, king, king.
That's right, baker. The writer says, "…therefore God has blessed you forever." (Psalm 45:2) That's a long blessing. I've had cookies that didn't last till dinner, so forever sounds WILD to me.

This one is actually true. The writer tells the king, "…therefore God has blessed you forever." (Psalm 45:2) The word that matters is forever. It's no short-term blessing, friend, and there's no expiration date stamped on it.
Yes! The writer says, "Strap your sword at your side, O mighty warrior…" (Psalm 45:3) A sword on the hip and a title like that. This is not a king who spends the day folding napkins.

Good guess, since shepherds show up all over the Bible. But in this verse the writer says, "Strap your sword at your side, O mighty warrior…" (Psalm 45:3) A sword is the clue. Shepherds carry a staff, and I don't think anybody straps a sword on for sheep duty.

I see why you'd pick judge, since justice comes up in this psalm. Still, verse 3 says, "Strap your sword at your side, O mighty warrior…" (Psalm 45:3) The sword points to a warrior. A judge wouldn't be told to strap one on, and the courtroom would get awkward fast.

Not quite, friend. The nations don't drive him back at all. The writer says, "Your arrows pierce the hearts of the king's foes; the nations fall beneath your feet." (Psalm 45:5) They fall, they don't rise. It's the opposite of a comeback story.

Right, it's false. The text says, "Your arrows pierce the hearts of the king's foes; the nations fall beneath your feet." (Psalm 45:5) No one is driving the king back here. The nations are the ones who end up under his feet.

You got it, baker. The writer says, "…justice is the scepter of Your kingdom." (Psalm 45:6) A scepter is what a king holds, and this king holds justice. That tells you a lot about how this kingdom runs.

Strength sounds like a good fit for a king with a sword. But the writer says, "…justice is the scepter of Your kingdom." (Psalm 45:6) The scepter is justice, plain and simple. Strength shows up in the verses around it, just not here.

I get it, with all that gold and ivory in this psalm, wealth feels likely. But verse 6 says, "…justice is the scepter of Your kingdom." (Psalm 45:6) The thing this king holds up is justice. The gold is nice, but it's not the scepter.

explanations.answer: He loved righteousness and hated wickedness
explanations.explanation: That's the one, friend. The psalm says, "You have loved righteousness and hated wickedness; therefore God, your God, has anointed you above your companions with the oil of joy." (Psalm 45:7) The word therefore ties the two together. The joy follows the love of what's right.

explanations.answer: He was the strongest of all his companions
explanations.explanation: Strong is a fair guess with all that sword talk. But the psalm gives a different reason: "You have loved righteousness and hated wickedness; therefore God, your God, has anointed you…" (Psalm 45:7) It never says he won a strength contest. The anointing comes after what he loved and hated.

explanations.answer: He was born the oldest son of a king
explanations.explanation: That would make a neat reason, but the text doesn't say it. The psalm says, "You have loved righteousness and hated wickedness; therefore God, your God, has anointed you above your companions with the oil of joy." (Psalm 45:7) Birth order never comes up. The reason given is what he loved and what he hated.
Yes, glad! The writer says, "…from palaces of ivory the harps make you glad." (Psalm 45:8) Harps, ivory palaces, and fragrance everywhere. That's a whole mood, baker.

Whoa, nobody's getting scared by harp music here. The writer says, "…from palaces of ivory the harps make you glad." (Psalm 45:8) These harps are there to lift the king up. Not a single scary violin in sight.
I know, some of us get sleepy at a concert. But verse 8 says, "…from palaces of ivory the harps make you glad." (Psalm 45:8) The harps bring gladness, not a nap. Keep your eyes open, friend!

That's right, friend. The writer says, "…the queen stands at your right hand, adorned with the gold of Ophir." (Psalm 45:9) She's right there at his side, dressed in gold. That's a spot you don't get by accident.

Nice thought, but his mother isn't mentioned in this verse. It says, "…the queen stands at your right hand, adorned with the gold of Ophir." (Psalm 45:9) The queen is the one in that spot. The text doesn't say who anyone's mother is.

Good try, baker, but a sister never appears in this psalm. The verse says, "…the queen stands at your right hand, adorned with the gold of Ophir." (Psalm 45:9) The queen holds that place. Gold of Ophir, by the way, is the fancy kind.

You got it. The writer says, "Forget your people and your father's house, and the king will desire your beauty…" (Psalm 45:10-11) Notice the king is the one who desires. The song says it plainly, no riddles needed.
Not this time. The writer says, "…and the king will desire your beauty…" (Psalm 45:11) Nothing about sending her away. The song points the other direction, toward the king wanting her close.

Whoa, friend, that's a sad ending, and it's not in the text. The writer says, "…and the king will desire your beauty…" (Psalm 45:11) Nobody's forgetting anything about her. The king is looking right at her.
Yes, favor! The writer says, "…men of wealth will seek your favor." (Psalm 45:12) Rich folks lining up to be on her good side. I just want people to like my cookies, and I'm not even rich.

Yikes, that's a sharp turn. The verse is kinder: "…men of wealth will seek your favor." (Psalm 45:12) The wealthy come to her, and they come looking for her good side. Nobody's seeking harm in this verse.

Gold fits the mood, since this psalm is shiny all over. But verse 12 says, "…men of wealth will seek your favor." (Psalm 45:12) The Daughter of Tyre brings a gift, but what the wealthy men seek is her favor. They're after her good graces, not gold.
Right on, baker. The text says, "In colorful garments she is led to the king…" (Psalm 45:14) Every step of this song heads toward the king. Colorful garments, too, and I'm a rainbow fan myself.

Good thought, since this is a song from a family of Levites. But the verse says, "In colorful garments she is led to the king…" (Psalm 45:14) She's headed to the king. The temple doesn't come up in this part.

A garden walk sounds lovely, friend, but it isn't in the text. The verse says, "In colorful garments she is led to the king…" (Psalm 45:14) The destination is the king. No flowers on this route that the song mentions.

Not quite, baker. The text says, "They are led in with joy and gladness; they enter the palace of the king." (Psalm 45:15) There's no fear and no trembling anywhere. It's a happy entrance from start to finish.

Right, it's false. The song says, "They are led in with joy and gladness; they enter the palace of the king." (Psalm 45:15) Joy and gladness, not fear and trembling. Walk in like that and even the doors would smile.

Yes, friend! The writer says, "…you will make them princes throughout the land." (Psalm 45:16) The line before it says sons will succeed their fathers. It's a promise that stretches way down the road.

Actually that's true. The writer tells the king, "Your sons will succeed your fathers; you will make them princes throughout the land." (Psalm 45:16) Princes throughout the land, no less. That's a lot of crowns to keep track of.

That's it, baker. The writer says, "…therefore the nations will praise you forever and ever." (Psalm 45:17) Because the name is remembered, the praise keeps going. Forever and ever is a long time to keep a song going.

I see why, with all those arrows earlier. But the last verse says, "…therefore the nations will praise you forever and ever." (Psalm 45:17) The song ends on praise, not fear. It closes on a happy note, friend.

Obey is a reasonable guess for a king's song. Still, the final verse says, "…therefore the nations will praise you forever and ever." (Psalm 45:17) The word is praise. That's how the whole song wraps up.
